title: Sell Mineral Rights in Sistersville, WV
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Sistersville, WV
metaDescription: Sistersville, Tyler County mineral owners: the historic 1890s oil-boom deed record, modern Marcellus/Utica units, and deep heirship title work.
heroLead: Sistersville was one of the busiest oil boomtowns in the country in the 1890s, and its mineral title record still reflects that dense, chaotic era of drilling and dealmaking.
intro: For a stretch of the 1890s, Sistersville's riverfront was packed with derricks and its streets with oil-money speculation, generating a volume of leases, severances, and assignments that few other West Virginia towns can match. That boomtown-era deed record, still on file at the Tyler County Courthouse, underlies much of the mineral ownership around Sistersville today — layered now with modern Marcellus and Utica/Point Pleasant horizontal development.

sections.heading: Tracing title through the 1890s boom
paragraphs: Because so many transactions happened in such a short window during the boom, a Sistersville-area mineral interest can have a genuinely complex early chain of title — tracts subdivided and re-subdivided, leases assigned multiple times within a few years, and deed language written in conventions that look very different from a modern instrument. Working through this record takes a real courthouse pull, not a quick database search.

It's also common to find a break somewhere in that chain — an assignment that was never recorded, or an heir who inherited without a formal probate — which is exactly the kind of gap a title review is built to catch before a sale closes.

sections.heading: Modern Marcellus and Utica development on historic ground
paragraphs: The same acreage that produced oil in the 1890s now sits within reach of horizontal Marcellus and Utica/Point Pleasant units, as Tyler County has developed as core stacked-pay territory over the past decade and a half. Mapping a boom-era deed description onto a current unit plat requires reconciling two very different surveying conventions.

sections.heading: Generations of heirs from a single boomtown-era severance
paragraphs: It's not unusual for a Sistersville-area mineral interest to trace to a single severance from the 1890s or early 1900s, now split among dozens of descendants scattered well beyond Tyler County. We buy individual heir shares directly, which is often the practical way forward when a family group this large has no realistic path to full consensus.

faqs.question: Why is Sistersville's deed record so much denser than other West Virginia towns its size?
faqs.answer: The 1890s oil boom generated an extraordinary volume of leases and transfers in a compressed period, all recorded at the Tyler County Courthouse, giving the area an unusually thick historical title record.

faqs.question: Could my Sistersville-area interest be under both Marcellus and Utica units?
faqs.answer: Possibly, given Tyler County's stacked-pay geology. Checking your division orders and any unit filings against both formations confirms whether you have one royalty stream or two.

faqs.question: How do I know if there's a break in my chain of title from the boom era?
faqs.answer: A title review tracing the deed books forward from the original severance is the only reliable way to catch a missing assignment or unprobated estate before it becomes a problem at closing.

faqs.question: My family's Sistersville interest is split among many distant relatives — can I still sell my share?
faqs.answer: Yes, you can sell your own documented fractional interest without needing every relative located or in agreement.
